title_en: Hong Kong Kunli Development Co., Ltd. and Jingze Co., Ltd. v. Zhanjiang Customs — dispute over administrative penalty decision
keywords_en: administrative; administrative penalty; first instance; intermediate people's court; Guangdong Province; legal person; state organ; Customs Law; Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law; determination of smuggling; lawful evidence; plaintiff standing; maritime transport; smuggled goods; customs seizure; administrative litigation
full_text_en:
Hong Kong Kunli Development Co., Ltd. and Jingze Co., Ltd.

v.

Zhanjiang Customs Administrative Penalty Decision

Plaintiff: Hong Kong Kunli Development Co., Ltd.

Legal Representative: Chen Junkang, Manager.

Agent ad litem: He Peihua, Lawyer, Legal Department, Guangdong Branch, China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.

Agent ad litem: Ying Songnian, Professor, China University of Political Science and Law.

Plaintiff: Hong Kong Jingze Co., Ltd.

Legal Representative: Guan Chengguo, Chairman.

Agent ad litem: He Peihua, Lawyer, Legal Department, Guangdong Branch, China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.

Agent ad litem: Chen Guoxun, Director and Manager of the Company.

Defendant: Zhanjiang Customs, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Li Songkun, Customs Director.

Agent ad litem: Fang Ning, Lawyer, Guangdong Foreign Economic Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Liu Guozhu, Officer, Zhanjiang Customs.

Third Party: Chen Dalu, Captain of the vessel "Lanjiang 04" owned by Haihe Transportation Company, Nghia Tinh Province, Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Agent ad litem: Tian Wenchang, Lawyer, Beijing No. 6 Law Firm.

Third Party: Hong Kong Zongjin International Development Co., Ltd.

Legal Representative: Chen Qihua, Manager.

Agent ad litem: He Peihua, Lawyer, Legal Department, Guangdong Branch, China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.

The plaintiffs, Hong Kong Kunli Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Kunli Company") and Jingze Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Jingze Company"), dissatisfied with the administrative penalty decision of the Zhanjiang Customs of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Zhanjiang Customs"), and claiming to be the owners of the confiscated property, filed a lawsuit with the Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province. After reviewing the plaintiffs' complaint, the Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court found that Chen Dalu and Hong Kong Zongjin International Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Zongjin Company") had an interest in the specific administrative act being challenged, and, pursuant to Article 27 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, notified them to participate in the proceedings as third parties.

The Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court, through trial, found the following facts:

On July 14, 1991, the third party, Chen Dalu, while navigating the vessel "Lanjiang 04" in China's territorial sea (at longitude 109°58'E, latitude 20°25'N), was transporting goods restricted for import into China, including: 1,216 "Mitsubishi" brand air conditioners, 70 "National" brand air conditioners, 2 "Casio" Chinese-English typewriters, 10 "Aiwa" brand laser disc players and VCRs, 10 two-way radios, 126 "Canon" photocopiers, 5,988 boxes of "Li Li Cheng" juice drinks, 230 14-inch color monitors, and 2 "Kenwood" audio systems. These were seized by the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs. On August 12, 1991, the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs, issued Penalty Notice No. (91) Zhan Guan Cha Zi 076, determining that the above goods transported by Chen Dalu lacked legal documentation, were ostensibly destined for Haiphong, Vietnam, but were actually intended for delivery at Beihai, Guangxi, and Shajing, Qinzhou, Guangxi, and that his actions constituted smuggling under Article 49, paragraph 2 of the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Customs Law") and Article 4, item (2) of the Implementing Rules for Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Implementing Rules"). Pursuant to Article 5, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Implementing Rules, it was decided to confiscate all of the above smuggled goods.

To support its penalty decision regarding the facts found and legal basis, the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs, submitted the following evidence and normative documents to the court: 1. A charter party dated May 29, 1991, between Hong Kong Kangning Development Trading Company (hereinafter "Kangning Company") and Haiphong Shipping Co., Ltd., Vietnam (hereinafter "Haiphong Company"). The contract stipulated that Kangning Company was the charterer, leasing the vessel "Lanjiang 04" (which belonged to the Haihe Transportation Company of Nghia Tinh Province, Vietnam, and had been sub-chartered to Haiphong Company), with Haiphong Company as the shipowner. Loading was at a safe berth in Hong Kong, and discharge was at a safe berth in Guangxi, China, with a time frame of June 10 to 15. 2. A supplementary agreement dated July 10, 1991, between Kangning Company, Le Dazhou of Haiphong Company, and Captain Chen Dalu of the "Lanjiang 04," stating: "In the second voyage of the main charter party (charter party of May 29), clause three mentions a safe berth in Guangxi, China, but there is an additional 99.5 CMB of cargo to be loaded/discharged at buoy no. 7, Shajing. Kangning Company requires the vessel to load/discharge at this location. If any incident occurs, Kangning Company will be responsible for resolving the dispute." 3. A letter from the shipowner to Kangning Company demanding payment of freight. This letter referred to the current voyage of the "Lanjiang 04" as the second voyage under the charter party with Kangning Company and demanded that Kangning Company pay freight and a guarantee deposit as per the original charter party, failing which the captain would refuse to sail. A representative of Kangning Company signed this letter on July 10, guaranteeing that the fees demanded by the shipowner would be remitted to the bank and requesting the vessel to sail on time on July 11. 4. Three nautical charts used by the "Lanjiang 04" for this voyage, showing the route from Hong Kong to Beihai, Guangxi, and the discharge locations, consistent with the charter party and the actual route taken by the vessel. The charts bore the signature and fingerprint of Nguyen Van Mu, Second Officer of the "Lanjiang 04," made after the vessel was seized. 5. A delivery instruction. A note written on Kangning Company letterhead was found on board. The note stated: "Voyage dated July 10, 1991, vessel name Lanjiang 04, first discharge location Beihai buoy no. 5 B/L01; second discharge location Shajing buoy no. 7 B/C#02." 6. Telegrams and drafts found on board. Among these, a telegram to Haiphong Company on July 11 stated: "Advise that Lanjiang 04 departed at 2100 hours on the 10th, estimated arrival Beihai on the 13th. Request instructions." A telegram draft prepared on July 14 for the shipowner stated: "Vessel anchored at Liusha at 2400 hours on July 12 to avoid wind. Heavy winds, vessel nearly sank. Vessel grounded at 0800 hours on the 14th. Request immediately inform Kangning Company. Arrival at Beihai will be delayed." Another telegram draft on the same day stated: "Vessel 04 departed Hong Kong for Beihai, encountered Typhoon No. 6 while passing through Qiongzhou Strait." 7. Records of interviews with 24 crew members conducted by the defendant. The vast majority of the crew admitted that the port of destination for this voyage was Beihai, Guangxi. They further stated that this voyage and the previous voyage were both executed under the same charter party, and because this voyage added the discharge location at Shajing buoy no. 7 in addition to Beihai, Guangxi, a supplementary agreement had been signed with the charterer. The cargo manifest, bills of lading, and waybills, which were first presented to Customs showing Haiphong, Vietnam as the port of destination, were provided to them by Kangning Company, Hong Kong, for use in passing inspections along the route from Hong Kong to Beihai. The defendant, Zhanjiang Customs, believed that the evidence from these seven aspects was sufficient to prove that the destination of the goods carried by Chen Dalu was Beihai and Qinzhou, Guangxi, and not Haiphong, Vietnam. 8. Article 49, paragraph 2 of the Customs Law and Article 4, item (2) of the Implementing Rules provide that transporting, purchasing, or selling goods or articles restricted by the State from import or export within China's inland waters or territorial sea, without legal documentation, shall be deemed an act of smuggling. Article 5, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Implementing Rules provides that for smuggling goods or articles restricted by the State from import or export, the smuggled goods or articles and illegal gains shall be confiscated, and a fine of up to the equivalent value of the smuggled goods or articles may also be imposed. The defendant argued that the penalty decision was legally sound and appropriate.

Furthermore, the defendant argued that the plaintiffs had no legal interest in the specific administrative act being challenged and thus lacked standing to sue. General Administration of Customs Document (89) Shu Diao Zi No. 500 interpreted the term "legal documentation" in the Customs Law to mean genuine transportation and commercial documents and materials held by the party that are consistent with the actual circumstances of the transported, purchased, or sold goods and articles and sufficiently prove their legality. Among these: (a) "party" means "the person in charge of the means of transport, the escort, and the cargo owner"; (b) "held" specifically means that the evidentiary materials must completely conform to the actual circumstances of the goods and articles, as well as the port of departure, port of destination, route of travel, and other related actions, and all entries must be fully consistent. In this case, the plaintiffs, Kunli Company and Jingze Company, were not the parties to whom the specific administrative act was directed. The evidentiary materials they submitted to the court were not the documents presented to Customs by the party at the time of the seizure. Therefore, they lacked plaintiff standing and had no right to sue. The court should dismiss the plaintiffs' complaint.

The evidence submitted to the court by the plaintiffs and the third parties included: 1. Sales and purchase contracts, bills of lading, waybills, packing lists, mate's receipts, and invoices between the plaintiffs and third party Zongjin Company and Haiphong Company, Vietnam. The dates on these documents were March, May, and July 1991, and their content indicated that the goods on the "Lanjiang 04" belonged to the plaintiffs and Zongjin Company and were destined for Haiphong, Vietnam. 2. Statements by Captain Chen Dalu of the "Lanjiang 04" and escort Le Dazhou. The statements claimed that the "Lanjiang 04" entered Chinese waters to avoid a typhoon, and that under duress from Chinese Customs officers, the crew were forced to admit that the voyage was destined for Beihai and Qinzhou, Guangxi, for discharge, and were compelled to sign pre-prepared texts. In summary, the plaintiffs and third parties argued that the defendant Zhanjiang Customs was wrong in finding that the goods transported on the "Lanjiang 04" lacked legal documentation and constituted smuggling. The court should quash the Penalty Notice No. (91) Zhan Guan Cha Zi 076, order the defendant to return all goods, and compensate for all losses incurred.

The Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court held that the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs, finding that the third party, Chen Dalu, lacked legal documentation for transporting these goods in China's territorial sea, was contrary to the facts; the finding that the goods were ostensibly destined for Haiphong, Vietnam, but actually for delivery at Beihai, Guangxi, and Shajing, Qinzhou, Guangxi, lacked factual basis; and the finding that Chen Dalu's actions constituted smuggling under Article 49, paragraph 2 of the Customs Law and Article 4, item (2) of the Implementing Rules was insufficiently supported by evidence. The evidence provided by the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs, could not negate the legality of the goods held by the plaintiffs and the third party Zongjin Company, nor could it negate the legality of the third party Chen Dalu's transportation of these goods through China's Qiongzhou Strait. The plaintiffs, Kunli Company and Jingze Company, held bills of lading, which are valid documents of title to the goods. The plaintiffs, believing that the specific administrative act of the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs, infringed on their ownership rights, had the right to file a lawsuit with the People's Court pursuant to Article 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The defendant's argument that the plaintiffs had no direct legal relationship with the specific administrative act being challenged was inconsistent with the facts. This claim was unfounded and was rejected. Accordingly, the court, pursuant to Article 54, item (2) of the Administrative Procedure Law, entered judgment quashing the Penalty Notice No. (91) Zhan Guan Cha Zi 076 of the defendant, Zhanjiang Customs; all goods confiscated under that notice were to be returned in full to the plaintiffs and the third party Zongjin Company.

Zhanjiang Customs, dissatisfied with the judgment of the Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court, appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court. It argued: The appellant had presented sufficient evidence at first instance to prove the facts found in the penalty decision. The first-instance judgment erred in finding that the evidence supporting the appellant's penalty decision notice, which found that "the goods transported by Chen Dalu, ostensibly destined for Haiphong, Vietnam, were actually destined for Beihai and Qinzhou, Guangxi, lacked legal documentation," was insufficient; and in finding that the penalty decision's application of Article 5, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Implementing Rules constituted an error in the application of laws and regulations, which was contrary to the facts. The laws and regulations applied in the appellant's penalty decision were correct. The appellant requested the court of second instance to set aside the first-instance judgment and uphold its penalty decision.

The Guangdong High People's Court, upon trial, held that the following evidence submitted by the appellant, Zhanjiang Customs, at first instance met the requirements for lawful evidence and had probative value: the charter party, the supplementary agreement, the letter from the shipowner to Kangning Company dated July 8, the letter with guarantee opinions signed by a representative of Kangning Company on July 10 specifying the delivery location by latitude and longitude, all bearing the signatures and fingerprints of Chen Dalu and Le Dazhou; a sent telegram draft and two unsent telegram drafts during the vessel's anchorage, bearing the signatures and fingerprints of radiomen Zheng Wenming and Hu Chun'an; and three nautical charts showing the route from Hong Kong to Beihai, Guangxi, bearing the signature and fingerprint of Nguyen Van Mu. The records of interviews with crew members submitted by the appellant were obtained in accordance with case handling procedures. Each record noted the time and place of the interview, was conducted with the assistance of an interpreter, and after the interviewees confirmed the accuracy of the records, they signed and fingerprinted both the Chinese and Vietnamese versions. The respondents (the plaintiffs below) alleged that the appellant, Zhanjiang Customs, obtained the interview records through intimidation, but they did not provide specific evidence, and upon investigation by this court, no intimidation was found. Therefore, these interview records were all lawfully obtained evidence and had evidentiary effect. The above evidence corroborated each other and fully proved that the goods transported by Chen Dalu were destined for delivery at Beihai and Qinzhou, Guangxi. The three original bills of lading, one cargo manifest, and two shipping documents on board the "Lanjiang 04" either lacked any signature or company seal, or bore only a single party's signature and seal, thus lacking lawful evidentiary effect. Among these, the three original bills of lading were inconsistent with the original documentation and were not genuine or valid documents. The sales contracts and other documents submitted by the respondents Kunli Company, Jingze Company, and Zongjin Company at the time of filing the lawsuit were inconsistent with the documents held on board the vessel and therefore also lacked evidentiary effect. In summary, the appellant, Zhanjiang Customs, based on the fact that, upon inspection of the "Lanjiang 04," the vessel failed to produce legal documentation for the goods on board, made its penalty decision in accordance with the law. The facts were clearly found, the evidence was conclusive and sufficient, the application of laws and regulations was correct, and the procedures were lawful. The penalty decision should be upheld. The first-instance judgment contained errors in fact finding and should be reversed. Accordingly, the Guangdong High People's Court, pursuant to Article 49, paragraph 2 of the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 4, item (2) and Article 5, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Implementing Rules, and Article 54, item (1) and Article 61, item (3) of the Administrative Procedure Law, on September 1, 1993, entered judgment setting aside the first-instance judgment and upholding the Penalty Notice No. (91) Zhan Guan Cha Zi 076 of Zhanjiang Customs.
